lessons.title: Working Capital Red Flags: Ballooning Receivables, Channel Stuffing and Stretched Payables

children.text: Every tool in this course works in reverse. The ratios you use to manage your own business are the ratios an investor, a lender or an acquirer uses to work out whether someone else's business is in trouble, and whether the trouble is being disclosed.

Working capital is where deterioration shows up first, because it is harder to manage than a profit figure. Revenue can be recognised early. Costs can be capitalised. But the cash either arrives or it does not, and the balance sheet records the gap.
The Pattern That Should Stop You
Here is five years of a company whose profit and loss statement looks excellent. Sales have grown 73%, margins are stable, and the business reports profit growth every year.

body.caption: Five years of a growing company (₹ crore)

body.title: Sales, receivables and inventory indexed to 100 in FY22

children.text: Receivables grew 146% while sales grew 73%, a ratio of 2 to 1. Receivable days went from 63.3 to 89.8. Inventory days rose too. And cash from operations fell every single year, turning negative in FY26 while the company was reporting record profits.

body.text: Now look at the cash conversion cycle row. It went from 89.4 days to 77.7 days, an apparent improvement. A screener showing only that row would suggest the business got better at working capital. It did not. Payable days rose from 78.2 to 130.4, and that stretching is masking the deterioration in the other two lines. Always read the three components separately.

stats.label: Receivables against sales
stats.context: The single most reliable early warning in working capital analysis

stats.label: Payable days
stats.context: Suppliers are funding the deterioration, which has a limit

stats.label: Cash from operations
stats.context: Profit is rising while cash is leaving

body.title: Compute the deterioration
body.prompt: Using the table above, what were the company's receivable days in FY26, with receivables of ₹128 crore and sales of ₹520 crore? Round to the nearest day.
body.explanation: ₹128 crore divided by ₹520 crore, times 365, is about 90 days, against 63.3 days five years earlier. On FY26 sales, those extra 26 days represent roughly ₹37 crore of additional cash locked in the receivable book.

children.text: Channel stuffing leaves a distinctive shape in quarterly numbers. Watch what happens around the year end at the same company.

body.title: Quarterly sales through the year end (₹ crore)

children.text: The fourth quarter carried 31.7% of annual sales, and the following quarter collapsed to below the first quarter of the previous year. That pattern, repeated annually, is the signature of
: stock pushed into the distribution channel to meet an annual target, which then has to be digested before the channel buys again.

markDefs.definition: Pushing more stock onto distributors near a period end than they can sell, which books revenue now and returns later as slow collections, returns or rebates.

body.text: One strong fourth quarter proves nothing. Indian businesses have genuine seasonality, from festive demand to the March rush in government and institutional orders. What is diagnostic is the combination: a fourth quarter spike, a first quarter collapse, receivable days rising at the year end, and the same shape repeating for three years.

body.title: Two explanations for the same numbers

columns.label: Benign
points: Receivables rose because a large new customer with longer terms was added
Inventory rose ahead of a launch or a known raw material price increase
Payable days rose because a supply chain finance programme was introduced
A weak quarter follows a strong one because of genuine seasonality
Management explains all of it in the commentary, with numbers

columns.label: Concerning
points: Receivables rose with no identified customer or terms change
Inventory rose while the oldest ageing buckets expanded
Payable days rose while the MSME dues line grew and interest accrued
Every fourth quarter spikes and every first quarter collapses, for years
The commentary discusses revenue growth and never mentions the cash

cards.definition: The classic. Compute the growth rate of each over three to five years and compare. A ratio above about 1.2 needs an explanation.
Operating cash flow persistently below operating profit means profit is being absorbed by the balance sheet.
Either genuine bargaining power, a supply chain finance programme, or liquidity stress. Only one of the three is good news.
The Schedule III ageing note showing growth in the one to two year and over three year buckets, especially in the disputed column.
Work recognised but not yet invoiced sits outside trade receivables and outside the ageing schedule, so it escapes both tests.
Amounts due from group entities parked in current assets, which are neither trade receivables nor recoverable on normal terms.
A residual line growing faster than the business usually contains something that deserves its own line.

cards.term: Inventory provisions flat while inventory grows
cards.definition: If stock rises for three years and the provision for slow-moving items does not move, someone has decided nothing ever gets old.
Growing margin money against letters of credit and guarantees means suppliers and banks are asking for more security.

body.title: Three places the auditor has to tell you something

children.text: Bank statements against books. Under clause 3(ii)(b) of

, where a company has working capital limits above ₹5 crore secured against current assets, the auditor must report whether the quarterly returns or statements filed with the banks agree with the books of account, and give details if they do not. This is a powerful disclosure: a company inflating stock or receivables in its monthly statements to protect drawing power now has that discrepancy reported.

markDefs.definition: The Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020, which requires auditors to report on specific matters, including whether quarterly statements filed with banks agree with the books.

children.text: The ageing schedules. Since the 2021 Schedule III amendments, both trade receivables and trade payables carry published ageing schedules, split between undisputed and disputed and between considered good and considered doubtful. Read the disputed column and the oldest buckets first, and read them across three years rather than one.

Emphasis of matter and qualifications. An auditor who is uncomfortable but not prepared to qualify will often say so in an emphasis of matter paragraph, frequently about recoverability of receivables or valuation of inventory. Auditor resignations mid-term deserve even more attention, since the reasons given are usually brief and the timing rarely is.

The extreme version of these patterns is fabrication. In the Satyam Computer Services fraud, disclosed by the chairman in 2009, the falsified figures included receivables and cash balances that did not exist. That case is unusual in being confessed and adjudicated, but the mechanism is ordinary: the balance sheet lines that are hardest to verify from outside are the ones most often used to absorb a gap.

body.text: Be careful with the conclusion you draw. Almost all of these flags have innocent explanations, and most companies showing one or two of them are simply managing a difficult year. What warrants real concern is a cluster: receivables outgrowing sales, cash conversion falling, payables stretching and ageing deteriorating, all at once, across several years, with no management explanation that uses numbers.

body.title: Which combination is most concerning?
body.question: You are reviewing four companies. Which pattern deserves the most scrutiny?
options: Receivable days rose from 45 to 52 in a year when a large new export customer was added on 90-day terms
Inventory days rose 15 days ahead of an announced raw material price increase, with management saying so in the commentary
Receivables grew twice as fast as sales for three years, cash from operations turned negative, payable days rose 50 days, and the fourth quarter carries a third of annual sales
Payable days rose 20 days after the company disclosed a new supply chain finance programme
body.explanation: The third option is a cluster rather than a single flag, sustained over years, with no benign explanation offered. The others each have a specific, disclosed reason, which is exactly what you look for when deciding whether a movement is deterioration or a decision.

body.title: The masking effect
body.textWithBlank: A cash conversion cycle can appear to improve even while receivables and inventory worsen, if ___ days are rising fast enough to offset both.
body.explanation: Stretching suppliers subtracts from the cycle, so it can mask deterioration in the other two components. This is why the three components must always be read separately rather than through the net figure.

body.title: The screening call
body.scenario: You are an analyst reviewing a mid-cap industrial company. Over four years sales grew 68%, profit after tax grew 74%, receivable days went from 58 to 79, inventory days from 71 to 84, payable days from 62 to 103, and cash from operations fell from ₹31 crore to ₹4 crore. The company has just announced a rights issue to fund capacity expansion. Management commentary highlights record order book and margin expansion, and does not mention working capital.
body.prompt: What is your read, and what would you ask management on the earnings call?
body.modelAnswer:
The read: the profit is real on paper but it is not converting to cash, and the business is funding growth through its suppliers while it waits for customers to pay.

Receivables and inventory are both rising faster than sales, and payables are rising faster still, which is the only reason the cycle has not blown out visibly. Operating cash flow falling from ₹31 crore to ₹4 crore while profit grew 74% is the finding that matters, because it means four years of reported profit have been absorbed by the balance sheet. The rights issue is the tell: a company generating cash does not usually need one to fund routine capacity.

What to ask management, in this order. First, what share of the receivable book is over 90 days, and how has that share moved over four years? Second, what explains payable days rising 41 days, and specifically whether a supply chain finance programme is in place, since that would change the interpretation completely. Third, how much of the rights issue proceeds will fund working capital rather than the capacity expansion described in the announcement? Fourth, what are the dues to micro and small enterprises, and has any interest been accrued under the MSMED Act? Fifth, what is the company's own target for the cash conversion cycle, and who owns it?

What the answers tell you. Specific numbers offered readily suggest a company that is managing a known problem. Vague answers about industry conditions and customer mix, especially on the ageing question, suggest nobody has looked. On a call, the quality of the answer to the first question usually settles the matter.

body.label: The single most useful test
body.context: Compute both over three to five years and divide. Above roughly 1.2, ask why, and do not accept an answer that does not contain numbers.

body.title: A working capital red flag screen
steps: Compare growth in receivables, inventory and payables with growth in sales over five years.
Read receivable, inventory and payable days as three separate series, never through the net cycle alone.
Divide cash from operations by operating profit for five years and look at the trend, not the level.
Open the receivables and payables ageing notes and read the oldest buckets and the disputed column.
Check whether unbilled revenue, related party dues and other current assets are growing faster than sales.
Compare quarterly sales patterns across three years for a recurring fourth quarter spike and first quarter collapse.
Read the auditor's report, including the CARO clause on whether bank statements agree with the books.
Check whether short-term borrowings are rising alongside profits.
Look for one cluster rather than one flag, and always ask what management says about it.

body.label: Run the screen on a real company
body.description: The Ratios section gives you the three day-counts over a decade, the Cash Flow section gives operating cash flow, and the Documents section links to the annual report where the ageing notes and auditor report live. That is the whole screen in one page.

body.text: Revenue can be recognised early and costs can be deferred, but cash either arrives or it does not. Working capital is where the difference between the two is recorded, which is why it is the first place to look and the last place to be reassured.

points: Receivables growing materially faster than sales, sustained over years, is the most reliable early warning in working capital analysis.
A cash conversion cycle can look stable or improving while receivables and inventory deteriorate, if payable days are stretching to offset them.
Falling cash conversion alongside rising profit means the balance sheet is absorbing the earnings.
Channel stuffing leaves a repeating signature: a fourth quarter spike, a first quarter collapse, and receivables rising at the year end.
Unbilled revenue, related party dues and a swelling other current assets line are where deterioration hides outside the ageing schedule.
CARO 2020 requires auditors to report whether quarterly statements filed with banks agree with the books, for working capital limits above ₹5 crore.
Almost every flag has an innocent explanation, so judge clusters across several years rather than single movements.
